title: Chapter 5
paragraphs: It was on a dreary night in November that I saw the result of my labors. With an anxiety bordering on agony, I gathered the instruments of life around me, ready to spark a glimmer of being into the lifeless thing at my feet. It was already one in the morning. Rain pattered dismally against the windows. My candle was nearly burned out. Then, by the flickering half-light, I saw the creature's dull yellow eye open. It drew a hard breath, and a convulsive movement shook its limbs.

How can I describe my feelings at this catastrophe? How can I capture the wretch I had worked so hard to create? His limbs were in proportion. I had chosen features I considered beautiful. Beautiful! Good God! His yellow skin barely covered the muscles and arteries beneath. His hair was lustrous black and flowing. His teeth were pearly white. But these fine details only made a more horrible contrast with his watery eyes — nearly the same color as the pale sockets they sat in — his shriveled complexion, and straight black lips.

The twists of life are not as changeable as human emotions. I had worked relentlessly for nearly two years with the sole purpose of bringing a lifeless body to life. I had sacrificed my rest and my health. I had wanted it with a passion beyond all moderation. But now that I was finished, the beauty of the dream vanished. Breathless horror and disgust filled my heart. Unable to bear the sight of the being I'd created, I rushed from the room. I paced my bedroom for a long time, unable to calm my mind enough to sleep. Eventually exhaustion overcame the turmoil I'd endured, and I threw myself on the bed fully clothed, trying to find a few moments of forgetfulness. But it was useless. I slept, but the wildest dreams tormented me. I thought I saw Elizabeth, glowing with health, walking through the streets of Ingolstadt. Delighted and surprised, I embraced her. But as I pressed my first kiss to her lips, they turned the color of death. Her features seemed to change, and I thought I was holding the corpse of my dead mother in my arms. A shroud wrapped her body, and I saw grave-worms crawling in the folds of the cloth. I woke with horror. Cold sweat covered my forehead. My teeth chattered. Every limb convulsed. Then, by the dim yellow moonlight forcing through the shutters, I saw the wretch — the miserable monster I had created. He was holding up the bed curtain. His eyes — if you could call them eyes — were fixed on me. His jaw opened. He mumbled some inarticulate sounds. A grin wrinkled his cheeks. He might have spoken, but I didn't hear. One hand reached out, seemingly to hold me, but I escaped and rushed downstairs. I took shelter in the courtyard, where I stayed for the rest of the night, pacing back and forth in the greatest agitation, listening intently, catching and dreading each sound as if it might herald the approach of the demonic corpse to which I had so miserably given life.

Oh! No mortal could bear the horror of that face. A reanimated mummy could not have been so hideous. I had looked at him while he was still unfinished — he was ugly then. But when those muscles and joints were brought to life, it became a thing such as not even Dante could have imagined.

I passed the night in wretchedness. Sometimes my pulse beat so fast and hard that I could feel every artery throb. Other times I nearly collapsed from exhaustion and extreme weakness. Mingled with the horror was the bitterness of disappointment. Dreams that had been my nourishment and comfort for so long had become my hell. The change was so sudden, the collapse so complete!

Morning — gray and wet — finally revealed to my sleepless, aching eyes the church of Ingolstadt with its white steeple and clock showing six o'clock. The porter opened the courtyard gates that had been my refuge through the night. I went out into the streets, walking quickly as if I were trying to avoid the wretch I feared would appear around every corner. I didn't dare return to my apartment. I felt driven to keep moving, though drenched by rain falling from a black, comfortless sky.

I kept walking like this for some time, trying to ease my mental burden through physical exercise. I wandered the streets with no clear idea of where I was going or what I was doing. My heart hammered with fear. I hurried on with irregular steps, not daring to look around:
Like one who, on a lonely road, walks on in fear and dread, and, having once turned round, walks on and turns his head no more, because he knows a frightful fiend is treading close behind him.
From Coleridge's "Ancient Mariner."

Continuing this way, I eventually came to the inn where carriages usually stopped. I paused, not knowing why, and stood for several minutes staring at a coach approaching from the other end of the street. As it drew closer, I recognized the Swiss coach. It stopped right where I stood. The door opened, and I saw Henry Clerval, who instantly jumped out. "My dear Frankenstein!" he cried. "How glad I am to see you! How lucky that you're here just as I arrive!"

Nothing could match my delight at seeing Clerval. His presence brought back thoughts of my father, Elizabeth, and all the beloved scenes of home. I grasped his hand. In an instant, I forgot my horror and misery. For the first time in many months, I felt sudden, calm, pure joy. I welcomed my friend with the greatest warmth. We walked toward my college. Clerval talked for some time about our mutual friends and his own good fortune in being allowed to come to Ingolstadt. "You can imagine," he said, "how hard it was to convince my father that all necessary knowledge isn't contained in the noble art of bookkeeping. I think he remained unconvinced to the end. His constant reply to my pleas was the same as the Dutch schoolmaster's in The Vicar of Wakefield: 'I have ten thousand florins a year without Greek, I eat heartily without Greek.' But his love for me finally overcame his dislike of learning, and he's let me set off on a voyage of discovery to the land of knowledge."
"It's wonderful to see you. But tell me, how did you leave my father, my brothers, and Elizabeth?"

"Very well and very happy, though a little worried because they hear from you so rarely. By the way, I plan to scold you on their behalf. But my dear Frankenstein," he continued, stopping short and studying my face, "I didn't notice before how terribly ill you look. So thin and pale — you look as if you haven't slept for days."

"You've guessed right. I've been so deeply occupied with one project that I haven't allowed myself enough rest, as you can see. But I hope — I sincerely hope — that all these labors are now finished and I'm finally free."

I trembled violently. I couldn't bear to think of, much less mention, what had happened the night before. I walked quickly, and we soon reached my college. Then the thought struck me — and it made me shiver — that the creature I'd left in my apartment might still be there, alive and walking about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. I begged him to wait a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs, then raced up to my room. My hand was on the lock before I caught myself. I paused, and a cold shudder ran through me. I threw the door open violently, the way children do when they expect a ghost waiting on the other side. But nothing was there. I stepped fearfully inside. The apartment was empty. My bedroom was free of its hideous occupant. I could hardly believe my luck. When I was sure my enemy had truly fled, I clapped my hands for joy and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room. The servant soon brought breakfast, but I couldn't contain myself. It wasn't just joy that possessed me. My skin tingled with excess sensation. My pulse raced. I couldn't stay still for a single moment. I jumped over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed aloud. Clerval first attributed my wild spirits to happiness at his arrival. But when he looked more closely, he saw a wildness in my eyes he couldn't account for. My loud, uncontrolled, heartless laughter frightened and bewildered him.
"My dear Victor," he cried, "what in God's name is the matter? Don't laugh like that. You're ill! What's causing all this?"

"Don't ask me," I cried, covering my eyes, for I thought I saw the dreaded specter glide into the room. "_He_ can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!" I imagined the monster seizing me. I struggled wildly and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A reunion he'd looked forward to with such joy had so strangely turned to bitterness. But I didn't witness his distress, for I was unconscious and didn't recover my senses for a long, long time.

This was the beginning of a nervous fever that confined me for several months. During all that time, Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that, knowing my father's age made a long journey inadvisable and how much my illness would distress Elizabeth, he spared them this grief by hiding how sick I really was. He knew I couldn't have a kinder or more attentive nurse than himself. Confident I would recover, he believed that rather than doing harm, he was performing the kindest possible act toward them.

But I was genuinely very ill. Only Henry's limitless, tireless care could have brought me back to life. The image of the monster I'd created was constantly before my eyes. I raved endlessly about him. My words must have puzzled Henry. At first he took them for the wanderings of a fevered mind. But my persistent return to the same subject convinced him that my illness truly had its origin in some strange and terrible event.

Very slowly, with frequent relapses that alarmed and grieved my friend, I recovered. I remember the first time I could look at the world around me with any kind of pleasure. I noticed that the fallen leaves had disappeared and young buds were sprouting from the trees outside my window. It was a divine spring, and the season greatly helped my recovery. I felt joy and affection revive in my heart. My gloom faded. Soon I was as cheerful as I'd been before that fatal passion seized me.

"Dearest Clerval," I exclaimed, "how kind, how incredibly good you are to me. Instead of studying this whole winter as you'd planned, you've spent it in my sick room. How can I ever repay you? I feel terrible about the disappointment I've caused you. But please forgive me."
"You'll repay me completely if you just get well as fast as you can and don't upset yourself. Since you seem to be in such good spirits, may I mention one thing?"
I trembled. One thing! What could it be? Could he be hinting at a being I didn't dare even think about?

"Relax," said Clerval, noticing my change of color. "I won't bring it up if it upsets you. But your father and cousin would be very happy to receive a letter from you in your own handwriting. They barely know how ill you've been, and your long silence has worried them."
"Is that all, dear Henry? How could you think my first thought wouldn't fly to those dear, dear friends I love and who deserve my love so much?"
"If that's how you feel, you'll perhaps be glad to see a letter that's been waiting here for you for some days. It's from your cousin, I believe."
